common_name: Kaimon Dake Leopard Plant (Dwarf White-Variegated Selection)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; a little filtered morning sun sharpens the white variegation on 'Kaimon Dake' without scorching the leaves.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, siting plants where they can catch an hour or two of gentle morning light rather than deep, unbroken shade. 'Kaimon Dake' is a compact selection of leopard plant named for a Japanese mountain, prized for rounded leaves broadly edged in creamy white with dark green speckling concentrated toward the leaf centers; new growth emerges almost entirely white before gradually filling in with green as the foliage ages. Loose clusters of small yellow daisy-like flowers appear on short stalks in late fall into winter, well after most other shade perennials have finished for the season. Its smaller stature compared to species Farfugium makes it a good fit for containers, rock gardens, and the front of shaded borders; protect from hard freezes and give supplemental water during dry spells to keep the variegated foliage from browning at the edges.

common_name: Raulston Hardy Walter's Viburnum (Compact Cold-Hardy Boxwood Alternative)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring, summer, or fall in average, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Raulston Hardy' holds a tighter, denser habit than the straight species and needs little corrective pruning to stay bun-shaped.

directions: Site in average, moist, well-drained, acidic soil and water regularly through the first growing season; once established, this selection handles both short dry spells and occasional wet soil, along with heat, humidity, and light browsing pressure better than many broadleaf evergreens. 'Raulston Hardy' is a J.C. Raulston Arboretum introduction bred from the Southeastern native Walter's viburnum for extra cold tolerance, forming a dense, fine-textured, bun-shaped mound of small narrow leaves that stays evergreen to semi-evergreen and often takes on a purplish cast in cold weather. Clusters of small white flowers open in spring, sometimes with sporadic repeat bloom into fall, followed by small black drupes that draw songbirds. Its tight, uniform habit and reliable cold hardiness make it a low-maintenance native alternative to boxwood for hedges, foundation plantings, and mass plantings in partial shade to full sun.
